clue.text: Tired, chum? Let's call it a draw

parts.note: tired, as in worn out and lacking freshness, means stale
a chum is a friend, a mate

explanation.surface: Two weary friends agree to abandon their game and settle for a draw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let's call it a' is link padding that makes the surface a weary suggestion; the definition is the single word 'draw'.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess a position where neither side can move legally without check ends the game as a draw, so the word stands for any deadlock.

clue.text: Gets smaller lights

definitions.meaning: narrows gradually towards one end, a verb in the third person
thin candles or wax-coated wicks used for lighting

explanation.surface: Something shrinks as the lamps are dimmed.
explanation.definitionFit: A thing that narrows to a point does this, and slender candles used to carry a flame are also called by this name.

clue.text: Insect that's always plagued us

parts.note: a swarming grasshopper famous from the biblical plagues of Egypt and still devastating crops in vast swarms

explanation.surface: A complaint about an insect pest that has bothered humanity forever.
explanation.definitionFit: This grasshopper forms swarms that strip crops, one of the ten plagues in Exodus.

clue.text: On average, it pays to be sincere

parts.note: the mean is the average value of a set of numbers
taken as written

explanation.surface: A homily claiming that, on balance, honesty is the best policy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pays to' is link padding giving the moral-sounding surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To intend what one says seriously is an idiom for being genuine and honest.

clue.text: An irritant felt particularly by bush?

definitions.text: An irritant felt particularly by bush?

parts.words: An irritant felt particularly by bush?
parts.note: the idiom for a persistent annoyance, taken literally: a rose bush or bramble carries prickles along its flank

explanation.surface: Wondering who suffers most from a nagging annoyance.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'bush' is a literal shrub, which really does have spikes on its flanks.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a constant source of annoyance, pictured as a prickle lodged in the flank.

clue.text: Case in which the French show disapproval of jail

indicators.note: the second pieces sit inside the word for case, which is split open around them

parts.note: taken as written
la is the feminine form of 'the' in French
to boo is to jeer in disapproval

explanation.surface: A French court case where the crowd jeers at a prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in which' puts LA and BOO inside CASE, split as CA...SE.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang Americanism, from Spanish calabozo, for a prison or lock-up.

clue.text: He picks solid fuel

parts.note: someone who hacks at a seam with a pick to dig out the black fuel burned in grates; 'picks' also suggests choosing

explanation.surface: A man choosing which fuel to burn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picks' reads as selects, but the worker literally uses a pick underground.
explanation.definitionFit: A pit worker who digs out coal, traditionally with a pick.

clue.text: Church festival held by English at some expense

parts.note: pent, as in pent up, means held in or confined
an expense is a cost

explanation.surface: An English church celebration put on at considerable cost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held by' looks like a containment, but 'held' is PENT and the pieces simply line up; 'by' and 'at some' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Whitsunday, seven weeks after Easter, marks the descent of the Holy Spirit on the apostles.

clue.text: A hat for a gangster

parts.note: a cap is a kind of hat
a, as in a single one, means one

explanation.surface: A trilby chosen for a mobster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A hat' becomes CAP ONE, the way one might say 'cap, one' for a single cap.
explanation.definitionFit: Al, the Chicago mobster of the Prohibition era, is the most famous criminal of that name.

clue.text: He looks at a magazine

definitions.meaning: a person who watches an event, an onlooker
a long-running British weekly political and cultural periodical

explanation.surface: A man browsing a magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: An onlooker at a match is a watcher, and the British weekly review founded in 1828 carries that title.

clue.text: Just dance and dance — out of this world!

parts.note: a ball is a formal dance
ET stands for extraterrestrial, a being from beyond this world

explanation.surface: An enthusiastic urge to do nothing but dance, it's heavenly!
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of this world' looks like praise but is the alien, ET; 'Just dance' means dance alone, without speech or song.
explanation.definitionFit: This theatrical art tells its story purely through movement and music, with no words.

clue.text: Germans put pressure on Soviets

parts.note: P is the symbol for pressure in physics
people of the Soviet Union, loosely Russians

explanation.surface: A Cold War headline about West Germany leaning on Moscow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put' and 'on' are links; Prussia was a German kingdom.
explanation.definitionFit: People of Prussia, the dominant state in the old German empire, were Germans.

clue.text: Signs of astrological activity

parts.note: the twelve star signs from Aries to Pisces taken as a set, the band of sky astrologers work with

explanation.surface: Evidence that horoscope-readers have been busy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Signs of' reads as evidence of, but it means the star signs themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: The band of the heavens divided into twelve star signs used in horoscopes.

clue.text: Very trim — and proud of it, we hear!

definitions.text: Very trim — and proud of it, we hear!

parts.words: Very trim — and proud of it, we hear!
parts.note: neat and orderly, with a jokey picture of a vessel, always called 'she', boasting of its figure, the whole sounding like a boat's outline

explanation.surface: Someone slim and pleased about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very trim' is the plain meaning; the rest jokes that the phrase sounds like a vessel's proud figure.
explanation.definitionFit: A nautical idiom for neat and in good order, as everything aboard a well-run vessel must be.

clue.text: High praise for an adult I love to tease

indicators.note: to tease out fibres is to pull them apart, so these letters are pulled apart and rearranged

parts.note: love is zero in tennis scoring, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: Flattery offered to a grown-up one likes to rib.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to tease' rearranges ANADULTI plus O (from 'love'); 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Excessive admiration or flattery heaped on someone is extreme praise.

clue.text: It denotes genuine quality

parts.note: the abstract noun naming the trait of being honest and heartfelt, rather than a hallmark on goods

explanation.surface: A label that guarantees authentic quality goods.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a hallmark of craftsmanship, but 'genuine quality' is the virtue of honesty.
explanation.definitionFit: Honesty and freedom from pretence are the quality of being genuine.

clue.text: Canal losing chlorine in equal quantities

indicators.note: losing tells us letters standing for chlorine are dropped from the word canal

parts.note: Cl is the chemical symbol for chlorine

explanation.surface: A waterway being purified of chlorine, measured out evenly.
explanation.walkthrough: CL is not one run in CANAL: C goes from the front and L from the back.
explanation.definitionFit: A pharmacists' term on prescriptions meaning of each ingredient the same amount.

clue.text: A long time in a state of savagery

indicators.note: in signals that the answer sits within the letters of savagery

explanation.surface: A long era spent in barbarism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a state of' is link padding; the letters sit in the middle of 'savagery'.
explanation.definitionFit: An era or eon is a lengthy period, as in 'I waited for ages'.

clue.text: A noun to delete, also

parts.note: N is the grammatical abbreviation for noun
D, short for dele, is the proofreaders' mark meaning delete

explanation.surface: An editor's note about a word to strike out as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is a link; the clue reads like proof-correction instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: A conjunction adding something further, like 'as well' or 'besides'.

clue.text: Taking no chances on recycling: "no tins", she begged

indicators.note: recycling reprocesses material into new form, so these letters are reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: A woman pleads to keep tins out of the recycling, playing safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on recycling' rearranges NO TINS SHE BEGGED; 'on' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means backing more than one outcome to avoid loss, so not risking anything.

clue.text: Finish to the south of Essex, maybe

definitions.text: to the south of Essex, maybe
definitions.meaning: Essex's seaside resort at the Thames estuary is named South plus this word, so it follows 'south' in Essex

explanation.surface: Ending up somewhere down in the south of Essex.
explanation.walkthrough: Southend-on-Sea is a resort town in Essex, the county east of London; 'maybe' flags the cryptic second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A close or conclusion, and the second part of the name of the Essex seaside town.

clue.text: They have a particular station in life

definitions.text: They have a particular station in life

parts.words: They have a particular station in life
parts.note: people whose working base is a station of their own, the building where officers report and suspects are held

explanation.surface: People who know their social rank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'station in life' means social standing, but here it is the literal station where officers are based.
explanation.definitionFit: The force works from its own station, the local headquarters of officers.

clue.text: Cute, though not noted for it

definitions.text: Cute, though not noted for it

parts.words: Cute, though not noted for it
parts.note: take the note TE from the word cute and CU is left, the chemical symbol of a reddish metal; also, police officers are not famed for being cute

explanation.surface: Someone attractive who never gets recognised for it.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing TE, a note in tonic sol-fa, from 'Cute' leaves CU, chemistry's symbol for this metal; it is also British slang for a police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: The reddish metal has the symbol Cu, and the word is also slang for a policeman.

clue.text: Small name for a small amount

parts.note: micro means very small

explanation.surface: A tiny label for a tiny quantity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A millionth of a metre, a minute unit of length.

clue.text: A trustee I take, with some hesitation, to court

parts.note: um is a sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: A nervous person bringing a trustee to court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take', 'with' and 'to' are links; 'court' means a courtyard, not a law court.
explanation.definitionFit: An open central hall or courtyard within a building, as in a Roman house.

clue.text: Spend time with a colleague

definitions.meaning: to keep company with someone, a verb
a partner or fellow worker, a noun

explanation.surface: Advice to socialise with a workmate.
explanation.definitionFit: To mix with people is to keep company, and a business partner or co-worker shares the word.

clue.text: They loathe cooking hearts

indicators.note: cooking a dish changes its ingredients, so these letters are reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: People disgusted by preparing offal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooking' rearranges HEARTS.
explanation.definitionFit: People who loathe are those who detest or despise, a plural noun matching 'They'.

clue.text: 1970s fashion clue that might be a red herring?

definitions.text: 1970s fashion clue that might be a red herring?

parts.words: 1970s fashion clue that might be a red herring?
parts.note: a very wide neckwear of that decade, named after a smoked herring; the red herring is a misleading clue, and a kipper is a smoked fish

explanation.surface: A fashion detail from the 1970s that turns out to be a false lead.
explanation.walkthrough: A red herring is a misleading clue in a mystery, and also a smoked fish like a kipper; the 1970s fashion is the very wide neckwear named after that fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A notably wide, garish necktie fashionable around 1970, named for the fish it resembled.

clue.text: In favour of not getting round quickly

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of

indicators.note: getting round means the word not is turned about and read backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who backs quick action but never gets around to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting round' turns NOT into TON.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal word, from Spanish, meaning at once or promptly.

clue.text: A strong ticker is what a player needs

definitions.text: A strong ticker is what a player needs

parts.words: A strong ticker is what a player needs
parts.note: a device that beats time loudly for a musician practising, rather than a healthy heart for an athlete

explanation.surface: A healthy heart is essential for a sportsman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ticker' is slang for heart and 'player' suggests a sportsperson; really it is the musician's clicking timekeeper.
explanation.definitionFit: A clockwork or electronic device that beats regular time for practising music.
